newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu struggles to keep coalition intact.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu struggles to keep coalition intact.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu is struggling to keep his coalition intact.
The Israeli prime minister defeated a parliamentary no-confidence motion on Tuesday -- but without support from 11 of 66 coalition members, including his own foreign minister.

He was also forced to put off naming a finance minister after his candidate, hard-liner Ariel Sharon, demanded a senior security post in addition to the appointment, sparking opposition among other cabinet ministers.
"These are signs of weakness. Netanyahu's government is now seen as extremely weak," said political analyst Gerald Steinberg.
Disgruntled coalition partners complain of mismanagement by Netanyahu, whose ill-fated appointment of an attorney general earlier this year nearly got him indicted.

Analysts said some cabinet members were also concerned the deadlock in peacemaking with the Palestinians, prompted by Netanyahu's settlement building in Arab East Jerusalem, would touch off another round of regional violence.

"I'm very happy that the no-confidence fell. I predicted as much. I told you that the government would hold," Netanyahu told reporters after his government defeated the motion by a 55-50 majority in the 120-member parliament.

Two legislators abstained in the vote which followed more than six hours of stormy debate. Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi's speech in defence of the government nearly cost Netanyahu the support of four additional coalition members.
Hanegbi caused a political storm by accusing legislator Ehud Barak, leader of the opposition Labour party and former army chief, of abandoning wounded soldiers during a 1992 training accident.
His rancorous speech prompted threats by members of the Third Way party to withhold their support.
"One or two more incidents like that and the people who abstained in this vote will vote against the government next time," Steinberg told Reuters. "I think it's a matter of time."

Earlier on Tuesday the prime minister's office said Netanyahu had delayed naming a finance minister after failing to come to terms with Sharon, architect of Israel's West Bank settlement boom in the early 1990s.

Sharon, 69, insisted Netanyahu let him join Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai and Foreign Minister David Levy in making up the Israeli leader's team of insiders who hammer out strategy in Arab-Israeli negotiations.
The post would be Sharon's first top security job since he was forced out as defence minister over a 1982 massacre of Palestinians.
"I stated (to Netanyahu) in a very clear fashion that I have to be on this team... that deals with political security issues," Sharon, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, told Israel Radio.
Political analysts said the burly ex-general was sure to get the post -- a move likely to alarm the Arab world and the United States, Israel's closest ally.
"There are still problems which we will solve in the future including the appointment of ministers," said Netanyahu.
His spokesman said the appointment, part of a cabinet shuffle, would be completed within days and brought for parliament's approval next week.

Levy and Mordechai, relative moderates in the rightist-religious government, were worried the appointment would yank the cabinet rightward at a time of rising tensions with the PLO over a three-month-old freeze in peace moves, the analysts said.

"This is something devastating for David Levy and Yitzhak Mordechai because they never wanted to share strategy and ideas with Sharon," Shimon Shiffer of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper said. "For the Americans and Palestinians, it's very scary."
